record.tranche_reason: The study reports that two acoustic neurons initially appeared to respond to one phoneme in maximally activating examples, but showed polysemantic behavior when examples at different activation ranges were examined. This refines the claim that inspection of activating examples establishes a neuron's job.
record.gate_note: The attention-window transcript results and decoder language-modeling results do not test any listed version. The study's general findings about interpretable encoder features do not measure the shares or conditions specified in the other versions.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, Whisper tiny's audio encoder, the authors report that two neurons looked like single-phoneme detectors from their maximally activating examples. Listening to examples at lower activation ranges showed polysemantic behaviour. That is a qualitative result on V6: an explanation fitted to top examples misses where the neuron fires. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The conclusion stresses that acoustic features are human interpretable and listenable, that encoder attention is localized, and that the decoder is a weak LM. It flags as a limitation that relying on dataset examples may bias the features found. The polysemantic-neuron finding appears in Section 1.3 but not in the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study listens to dataset examples across activation ranges rather than quantitatively testing explanation predictions on new activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Examining only maximally activating examples initially suggested single-phoneme responses; looking at different activation ranges revealed polysemantic behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: The first 50 neurons of encoder block.2.mlp.1 were labelled by inspecting max-activating examples. About 37 got a phoneme label and 3 non-phoneme sounds (white noise ×2, microphone); 10 were N/A (not interpretable). So about 80% looked interpretable by top-example inspection in a 39M audio encoder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Share of MLP neurons interpretable by max-activating-example inspection in a small speech encoder (Whisper tiny): about 80% of 50 sampled neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: The decoder's block.0.mlp.1 neurons fire on coherent semantic categories (food, ordinal numbers, motion verbs) in their max-activating examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decoder neurons of a speech-to-text model show monosemantic-looking semantic features in their top examples.

record.problems: The polysemantic-neuron result is reported for two neurons, with no numerical estimate of how common such neurons are. The authors note that using dataset examples may bias the features found.

untested.parts: No written explanation is scored on how well it predicts activations on held-out audio. The share of neurons that would be misread this way is not estimated; only neurons 1 and 3 are shown.
Qwen3-32B pole shares are not measured.
No language models, mixture-of-experts models or scale comparison.
No comparison of architectures, regularization or tools.

missing.what: Table of phoneme labels for neurons 0–49 of block.2.mlp.1, including 10 N/A neurons. This is a share of interpretable-looking neurons, though in an audio model that no version covers.
missing.versions: none (closest to V1/V2 but the model is not a language model)

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: this is a new setting with a qualitative result, not an argument that a version must be restated. The V6 support is weak (two neurons, no numbers). The record omitted the 50-neuron interpretability table.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole shares are not measured.
Whisper tiny is an audio-text model; the study does not measure neuron-job shares across language models, architectures, or scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or pose feature is tested.
The study does not compare architectures, regularization, tools, or interpretability shares.
No attribution graphs or reconstruction error are evaluated.
The study does not construct formal explanations and score their predictions on held-out activations; it examines sounds at different activation ranges.
No automated explanation scoring on new text is performed.
